Solution
Words: 93
i OurBigBook.com
The weight cancels the denominator in the Sturm-Liouville operator. Two integrations by parts, with real p,q, give the Lagrange identity for a Sturm-Liouville operator
⟨f,Lg⟩w​−⟨Lf,g⟩w​​=∫ab​[−f∗(pg′)′+(pf∗′)′g]dx=[p(f∗′g−f∗g′)]ab​.​
(1)
Thus the boundary form must vanish for every pair in the operator domain:
[p(f∗′g−f∗g′)]ab​=0.​
(2)
Separated real Robin boundary conditions As​y(s)+Bs​p(s)y′(s)=0 at s=a,b, with (As​,Bs​)=(0,0), make each endpoint contribution vanish. This includes Dirichlet boundary conditions and Neumann boundary conditions. Coupled conditions can also work: periodic y(a)=y(b) and p(a)y′(a)=p(b)y′(b) cancel the two endpoint contributions. For the regular problem, imposing a complete pair of such self-adjoint boundary conditions gives a self-adjoint differential operator; the displayed identity is the boundary-form criterion.

First, setting f=g=yn​ in the self-adjoint operator identity shows that λn​⟨yn​,yn​⟩w​ is real, so every eigenvalue is real. For two eigenfunctions,
λn​⟨ym​,yn​⟩w​=⟨ym​,Lyn​⟩w​=⟨Lym​,yn​⟩w​=λm​⟨ym​,yn​⟩w​.
(3)
Distinct eigenvalues therefore imply
⟨ym​,yn​⟩w​=∫ab​ym∗​yn​wdx=0.​
(4)
This is orthogonality of Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions.

The endpoint conditions become Y(0)=Y(1)=0. Multiplying −Y′′=(λ+1)Y by Y∗ and integrating shows that λ+1>0 for a nonzero solution. Put μ=λ+1​. The first endpoint selects Y=Asin(μt) and the second requires μ=nπ, n≥1. Hence
λn​=n2π2−1,yn​(x)=2​sin(nπlogx),n=1,2,….​

A single-valued potential must be 2π-periodic in θ. For a separated solution Φ=F(r)H(θ), the Laplace equation in polar coordinates becomes
Fr(rF′)′​=−HH′′​=μ.
(13)
The periodic angular eigenvalue problem has μ=n2, n≥0: its nonconstant eigenfunctions are cosnθ,sinnθ. Negative μ gives exponentials that cannot be periodic, and μ=0 gives only a constant angular factor. For n≥1, the radial Cauchy-Euler equation r2F′′+rF′−n2F=0 gives F=Arn+Br−n. At n=0 the two radial solutions are 1 and logr. Superposition therefore gives
Φ=A0​+B0​logr+n=1∑∞​[(An​rn+Bn​r−n)cosnθ+(Cn​rn+Dn​r−n)sinnθ].​
(14)
The expansion is interpreted on an annulus where the harmonic function is defined; particular boundary conditions determine its constants and convergence region. Single-valuedness is essential: allowing a cut in the angular domain would also permit nonperiodic angular solutions.

Solution

Words: 124
b OurBigBook.com
Treat each angular Fourier mode independently. Boundedness at the axis excludes the negative radial powers and the logarithm inside; decay at infinity excludes the positive powers, constant and logarithm outside. For the cosine mode write
Φn,in​=An​rncosnθ,Φn,out​=Bn​r−ncosnθ.
(15)
Continuity at R gives Bn​=An​R2n. The jump of the normal derivative is then
−nBn​R−n−1−nAn​Rn−1=−2nAn​Rn−1=−an​.
(16)
Thus An​=an​R1−n/(2n) and Bn​=an​Rn+1/(2n). The sine mode has the same relation with bn​. Therefore the potential of a charged cylindrical shell with angular Fourier data is
Φ(r,θ)=n=1∑∞​2nR​(an​cosnθ+bn​sinnθ){(r/R)n,(R/r)n,​0≤r≤R,r≥R.​​
(17)
There is no angular mean term: the given surface charge density has zero average. The interior constant is zero because its boundary value must match the vanishing exterior mean. A nonzero mean charge per unit length would instead produce a logarithmic electrostatic potential, incompatible with the specified decay at infinity.

Apply the product rule to the vector field Φ∇Ψ−Ψ∇Φ:
∇⋅(Φ∇Ψ−Ψ∇Φ)=ΦΔΨ−ΨΔΦ.
(18)
The gradient cross terms cancel. Integrating and applying the divergence theorem with outward unit normal n proves Green's second identity:
∫V​(ΦΔΨ−ΨΔΦ)dV=∮S​(Φ∂n​Ψ−Ψ∂n​Φ)dS.​
(19)
Choose the Dirichlet Green function GD​(r,r′) with Δr​GD​=δ(r−r′) and GD​=0 on S. Taking Ψ=GD​ and using the Dirac delta distribution, the left side becomes Φ(r′) while the second boundary term vanishes. Hence
Φ(r′)=∮S​f(r)∂nr​​GD​(r,r′)dS.​
(20)
The plus sign is tied to the convention ΔGD​=+δ, whose free-space fundamental solution is negative in three dimensions. The singularity may equivalently be handled by excising a small sphere about r′ before applying the smooth identity.

Write s=∣r′∣ and r′′=a2r′/s2. If ∣r∣=a, expansion of squared Euclidean distances gives
∣r−r′′∣2=s2a2​∣r−r′∣2.
(22)
Consequently ∣r−r′′∣=(a/s)∣r−r′∣, and the two terms in H cancel. This method of images gives the Dirichlet Green function inside a sphere:
H(r,r′)=−4π1​[∣r−r′∣1​−∣r−r′′∣a/s​].​
(23)
The image point is outside the sphere, so only the physical source contributes a Dirac delta distribution inside. As s→0, the image position tends to infinity and its coefficient also diverges, but their ratio has the finite limit
∣r−r′′∣a/s​⟶a1​.
(24)
Thus
H(r,0)=−4π∣r∣1​+4πa1​.​
(25)
The apparent singularity of the image construction at a central source is removable; the physical source singularity at r=0 remains.

Solution
Words: 111
i OurBigBook.com
Let r′=(x′,y′,−z′) be the reflection of the source in the equatorial plane. For a source in the upper half-ball, the Dirichlet Green function inside a hemisphere is
Ghemi​(r,r′)=H(r,r′)−H(r,r′).​
(26)
Both terms vanish on the spherical boundary. On the flat boundary z=0, the two source distances are equal, and the distances to their spherical image points are also equal, so the difference vanishes there too. The reflected physical source is in the lower half-ball and both inverted image points are outside the sphere. Therefore the only source singularity in the desired region is the original one, with coefficient +1 in ΔG. This combines reflection with the spherical method of images.

ii

Words: 157 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 157
ii OurBigBook.com
Reflecting repeatedly in the two parallel planes creates an infinite method of images. For r′=(x′,y′,z′), introduce
rn+​=(x′+4n,y′,z′),rn−​=(−x′−2+4n,y′,z′),n∈Z.
(27)
The Dirichlet Green function between parallel planes is
Gslab​(r,r′)=−4π1​n∈Z∑​[∣r−rn+​∣1​−∣r−rn−​∣1​].​
(28)
Each bracket is O(n−2), so the paired series converges absolutely away from the sources. At x=−1, reflection pairs the positive image indexed by n with the negative image indexed by −n. At x=1 it pairs that positive image with the negative image indexed by 1−n. The distances agree in each pairing, making both boundary values zero. This can be checked with symmetric finite partial sums first; the unmatched end terms tend to zero, so no subtraction of separately divergent series is needed. Only r0+​=r′ lies within the slab, so Δr​Gslab​=δ(r−r′). This is the usual Green function decaying at large transverse separation; such a condition selects the physical solution in the unbounded region.

A function is an analytic function at z0​ if it is holomorphic throughout some open neighbourhood of z0​, equivalently if it has a convergent power series there. In real components g=u+iv, continuous first partial derivatives in a neighbourhood together with the Cauchy-Riemann equations
ux​=vy​,uy​=−vx​​
(29)
throughout that neighbourhood are sufficient, and for an analytic function they hold there. Satisfying these equations only at the single point is not enough to establish analyticity in a neighbourhood.

Factor the polynomial denominator as (z−i)2(z+i)2. The numerator has values i and −i at the two roots, so neither cancels. Therefore
z=i and z=−i are double poles.​
(30)
The factor z−1/2 gives a branch point at zero, with local behaviour f(z)∼z−1/2. Infinity is also a branch point, since in the coordinate w=1/z the leading behaviour is f(1/w)∼w5/2. A single-valued branch requires a branch cut joining these points. Away from that cut and the two poles, the selected branch is holomorphic. For the integral below, use 0<argz<2π, putting the cut along the positive real axis.

Use a counterclockwise keyhole contour around the positive real branch cut, with small radius ε and large radius R. On the upper bank argz=0, so the integral tends to I. On the lower bank argz=2π, z1/2=−x​, giving the negative of the upper-bank integrand. That bank is traversed from R to ε, so its contribution also tends to I.
The outer circle contributes O(R−3/2), since f=O(R−5/2) and its length is O(R). The small circle contributes O(ε1/2), since f=O(ε−1/2). Both vanish. Hence
C=ε→0,R→∞lim​∮Γε,R​​f(z)dz=2I.​
(31)
The contour encloses both double poles ±i but excludes the branch point.

Use f​(ω)=∫R​e−iωtf(t)dt. Expanding each cosine into two exponentials and integrating its half-line gives
f​(ω)​=21​[λ−i(ω−2)1​+λ−i(ω+2)1​]+21​[λ+i(ω−1)1​+λ+i(ω+1)1​].​

ω−i2−i−2−i​Resy​i/5(−1+i)/16(1+i)/16​​

Insert this into (δik​+λXik​)Ykj​=δij​ and equate powers of λ. One obtains successively

det(K−zM)=−1004z3−108z2+613z−600​=0.
(59)
At the claimed z=6, this determinant is −27/50=0. Hence the printed claim that 6​ is a normal frequency is false for the stated data, and there is no corresponding nonzero normal mode.
The complete geometry-based answer is obtained from the three positive roots zj​:
4zj3​−108zj2​+613zj​−600(ωlow​,ωmiddle​,ωhigh​)​=0,≃(1.111471775, 2.491790287, 4.422172730).​​
(60)
An exact closed form for the squared angular frequencies is
zj​=9+3359​​cos[31​arccos3593/227453​​−32πj​],j=0,1,2.
(61)
They are approximately 19.555611657, 6.209018836 and 1.235369507, respectively. For any of these roots, a corresponding eigenvector can be chosen as
v(z)=​21​[(3−z/4)(1−2z/25)−1]1−2z/251​​.​
(62)
The last two rows of (K−zM)v=0 give this expression directly; the first is the characteristic equation. These three modes span all motion, with arbitrary sine and cosine amplitudes. Positivity of M and of the spring potential energy ensures that all squared angular frequencies are positive.
If instead one takes the PDF's printed I1​=m1​a2/6 as a stipulated inertia, then M=diag(1/2,1/4,2/25) and
det(K−zM)=−2002z3−69z2+626z−1200​.
(63)
The corresponding angular frequencies are approximately
(1.616170898, 3.315716400, 4.570997307).​
(64)
The same formula for v(z) applies, because its derivation used only the second and third rows. Here the determinant at z=6 is −63/25=0, so following the printed inertia does not repair the frequency claim. The PDF therefore needs a further correction to its numerical data or asserted frequency; the intended correction cannot be inferred uniquely.

i OurBigBook.com
Subtraction fails associativity: (0∗0)∗1=−1 but 0∗(0∗1)=1. Thus it violates the group axioms and is not a group. It has a right identity 0, but no element can be a two-sided identity element.

The operation is not defined for every pair in the proposed set: choosing a=1,b=−1 makes its denominator zero. Thus it is not even a binary operation on C∖{0}, and is not a group. In particular, removing zero from the domain does not prevent the sum in the denominator from vanishing.

iii OurBigBook.com
The substitution F(a)=ea, with F(−∞)=0, is a bijection onto [0,∞) and obeys
F(a∗b)=F(a)+F(b).
(65)
Thus the log-sum-exp function transfers nonnegative addition to the given set. It is closed, associative and commutative, with identity element −∞. But a finite a has ea>0, and adding a nonnegative number cannot give zero, so no finite a has an inverse element. Therefore it is a commutative monoid but not a group.

Solution
Words: 62
iv OurBigBook.com
The sum of two odd integers plus one is odd, so the operation is closed. Both associations of a triple give a+b+c+2, proving associativity. Its identity element is −1, and the inverse element of a is −a−2, also odd, since a+(−a−2)+1=−1. Thus it is an abelian group.
More explicitly, shifted addition on odd integers is ordinary integer addition in different coordinates:
F(a)=2a+1​,F(a∗b)=F(a)+F(b).​
(66)
This bijection is a group isomorphism to (Z,+).

For a subgroup H≤G and g∈G, the left and right cosets are gH={gh:h∈H} and Hg={hg:h∈H}. A normal subgroup satisfies gHg−1=H for every g. Multiplying this set equality on the right by g gives
gH=Hgfor every g∈G.​
(67)
Conversely this equality implies gHg−1=H, so it is an equivalent definition of normality.

G/H={gH:g∈G},(gH)(kH)=(gk)H.​

To check that this is well-defined, replace g,k by gh1​,kh2​ with h1​,h2​∈H. Their product is
gh1​kh2​=gk(k−1h1​k)h2​∈gkH,

since normality puts k−1h1​k in H. Hence the product does not depend on representatives. Associativity follows from that in G, the identity element is H=eH, and (gH)−1=g−1H. These verify the group axioms.
Lagrange's theorem counts the equal-sized cosets:
∣G∣=∣G/H∣∣H∣,∣H∣∣∣G∣.​

G≅Cp​ and G is abelian.​

Write a matrix in the set as M(a,b). The zero matrix M(0,0) has no multiplicative inverse matrix, so S is not a group. Its determinant is
detM(a,b)=∣a∣2+∣b∣2,
(72)
which vanishes only at that zero matrix. It is therefore the only element that needs to be removed.
For closure, direct matrix multiplication gives
M(a,b)M(c,d)=M(ac−bd∗, ad+bc∗).

The product of nonzero determinants is nonzero, so two nonzero elements never multiply to zero. The identity matrix is M(1,0), associativity is inherited from matrix multiplication, and
M(a,b)−1=∣a∣2+∣b∣21​(a∗b∗​−ba​)=M(∣a∣2+∣b∣2a∗​,∣a∣2+∣b∣2−b​).​

Thus S∖{02×2​} is a group​. It is the multiplicative group of nonzero quaternions in the complex matrix representation of quaternions.

a OurBigBook.com
Act on the four labelled vertices. A proper rotation gives an even permutation, identifying the rotational tetrahedral symmetry group with A4​, an alternating group. Geometrically there are one identity, three half-turns about opposite-edge midpoint axes, and two nontrivial rotations about each of four vertex-face axes. Therefore
∣G∣=1+3+8=12.​
(75)
The tetrahedral rotation conjugacy classes are
C0​C2​C+​C−​​elements in vertex notation{e}{(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)}{(123),(134),(142),(243)}{(132),(143),(124),(234)}​size1344​​​
(76)
To justify the splitting, the centralizer of a 3-cycle within A4​ is its three-element cyclic subgroup, so its conjugacy class has size 12/3=4. Its inverse is not conjugate to it in A4​: the permutations that reverse that cycle while preserving its fixed vertex are odd. Conjugating (123) by the even permutations produces the displayed C+​, and taking inverses gives C−​. The three half-turns are conjugate, since rotations move their axes into one another. Their centralizer has order four and their class therefore has size three.

Let
K={e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)}.
(77)
The product of any two distinct nonidentity elements is the third, and each squares to e, so K is a Klein four-group. Conjugating a double transposition simply relabels its letters, keeping it in the set. Hence K is a normal subgroup of A4​.
Choose r=(123). The cosets K,rK,r2K are distinct and cover the twelve elements. With ζ=e2πi/3, define
Φ(rjk)=ζj,j∈{0,1,2},k∈K.​
(78)
The coset decomposition makes this well-defined. Normality gives
(rjk)(rℓk′)=rj+ℓ(r−ℓkrℓ)k′∈rj+ℓK,
(79)
so Φ preserves products. It is onto {1,ζ,ζ2}≅C3​, and
kerΦ=K,A4​/K≅C3​.​
(80)
This is the tetrahedral quotient onto the cyclic group of order three. In terms of (a), it sends C0​∪C2​ to 1, C+​ to ζ, and C−​ to ζ2. The normality check above also follows abstractly because a group homomorphism kernel is normal.

The group is the direct product of groups Zp​×Zq​. Repeatedly adding (1,1) returns to (0,0) for the first time when both p and q divide the step number. Its order of a group element is therefore lcm(p,q). If p,q are coprime, this is pq, so it generates every element:
G(p,q)≅Cpq​.​
(81)
Explicitly, [t]pq​↦([t]p​,[t]q​) is the Chinese remainder theorem group isomorphism.
If d=gcd(p,q)>1, every pair satisfies
dpq​(n,m)=(0,0).
(82)
Thus every element order divides pq/d<pq, and no element can generate the whole group. Hence
G(p,q) is cyclic exactly when gcd(p,q)=1.​
(83)
This is the cyclicity of a product of two finite cyclic groups.

Thus there are ten subgroups: one trivial, five of order two, three of order four, and the whole group. The five order-two subgroups are mutually isomorphic. The two noncyclic order-four subgroups are mutually isomorphic Klein four-groups; neither is isomorphic to the cyclic group of order four.
For completeness, Lagrange's theorem permits only orders 1,2,4,8. An order-four subgroup containing U or U3 must be ⟨U⟩. Otherwise it can contain only I,U2 and elements UjV. The product of two distinct such elements is Uj−k. To avoid generating U or U3, their exponents must differ by two, giving exactly the two listed Klein four-groups. The order-two subgroups come from the five involutions U2 and UjV. This proves completeness.

For any cyclic subgroup H=⟨s⟩ of order n∈{1,2,4}, define
ρ1​(sj)=e2πij/n∈GL(1,C),ρ2​(sj)=(cos(2πj/n)sin(2πj/n)​−sin(2πj/n)cos(2πj/n)​)∈GL(2,R).​
(91)
Both preserve products because scalar phases and planar rotations add their angles. Each sends the generator to an element of exact order n, so both have trivial kernel and are faithful representations.
For ⟨U⟩≅C4​, take s=U: the generator images are i and R(π/2). For each order-two subgroup take its nonidentity element s; the images are −1 and −I2​. For the trivial subgroup the unique images are 1 and I2​, which are faithful on a one-element group.
The one-dimensional representation of C4​ here must use complex scalars. There is no faithful one-dimensional real representation of C4​, since a nonzero real scalar of finite order is 1 or −1, and neither has order four. The two-dimensional representations above are real.
